Question: What did you notice during an interview that made you not want the job?

When I arrived, she was there and told the manager: “I keep telling you we need one more employee, so I hired that girl.” He said alright and left. Second red flag: She started to show me what I would do and there were actually a lot of things to do: be the waitress, cook most of the meals (everything but the pizza), be the cashier, clean the place, clean the towels, etc. And all the male employees (and the manager) were mostly sitting and fooling around. He said “next week”, but she told him: “You already told me that last week and here you are, not paying me again!” I later asked the manager when I would get paid and he said I wouldn’t, as I wasn’t a “real” employee yet. I asked him when he would start paying me and he said after at least one month. I said that to my mother and she freaked out. Question: Why is it that Canadian French is so incomprehensible to the ears of a European?
Answer: Many languages have different varieties. These varieties are influenced by: It’s important to say it doesn’t mean we can’t understand each others though. I once had students from Cuba and from Colombia in my class and they were able to speak Spanish to each other and understand each other, even though their variety of Spanish wasn’t the same. It’s because every language has a “standard” register. A lot of people think it means there is “standard French”, which would be kind of worldwide, VS “Québécois French” (and other varieties). It’s not how it works. Every variety has its standard register, and these standard registers are all very close to each others, but aren’t exactly the same. Take a look at the picture. When the varieties are used in the formal register (soutenu), they get closer to each others. On the other hand, if they’re used in the casual register (familier), they get further from each others. If a Québécois uses the casual register, the probability a French or a Belgian won’t understand him is huge. But it’s not because of the French variety. It’s because of the register. So is Canadian French incomprehensible to the ears of a European? It depends on the register that is used. And the same can be said about any French variety. The Parisian slang is very hard to understand if used to a large amount. I visited France twice and I had no problem being understood, but in the same time, it was very clear for people I was talking to that I was Québécoise. So as you see, you can speak “Canadian French” and be understood by Europeans. The same thing happened in Belgium.

As an heterosexual woman, I have the privilege of not caring about how people will feel about my sexual orientation, because I will not be bullied or rejected because of that. I never had to “come out” as an heterosexual either. As a white person, it’s the same thing. The vast majority of people living in my town are white. When I watch TV or movies, I see white people all over the place. No one tell me I am a “terrorist” because of the colour of my skin. We all have a status, and some parts of that status usually make it easier for us. Being white is one of these characteristics that usually help. It doesn’t mean every person of colour experiment racism. It doesn’t mean they’re all doomed to misery and poverty. It just means there are more chances they’ll have to deal with a negative experience directly linked to the colour of their skin. I don’t know why I would be offended when someone tell me I am lucky enough that I won’t have to deal with that. That’s just the truth.

Question: Is German easy to learn for French speakers?
Answer: Knowing French definitely helps me a lot while I learn German, as does knowing English. English is great for the vocabulary. It took me a few minutes to learn to count in German, as the numbers sound the same as English. A lot of other words do to: trinken (to drink), gehen (to go), gut (good), Nacht (night), etc. French is sometimes good for the vocabulary too though: Krawatte (la cravate), Lampe (la lampe), Cousine (la cousine), etc. I think the pronunciation is probably much easier to master for a French speaker than it is for an English speaker. English is a “round” and not very much articulated language, but German and French are much more articulated. The letter [R] is kind of the same in French and German. I was already familiar will all German sounds, except the “ch” pronunciation. Is German easy though? No, it’s not, But it’s not as hard as I expected it to be. The hardest parts are: The conjugation and the grammar in general are not hard to learn, at least not for me. That is actually the part I enjoy the most.

Question: What phonetic articulations and other aspects of pronunciation would a French speaker from France have to change in order to pass as Québecois?
Answer: When I went to France, everyone knew right away I was Québécoise even though I did not speak casual French. There are things in the way we speak that betray us, even when we speak standard French. I will only talk about the standard Québécois French pronunciation (so no casual pronunciations), as this answer could go on forever if I also talk about the casual pronunciation, the vocabulary and the grammar (the grammar is mostly the same though, but there as some mistakes French do and Québécois don’t, and vice versa). For more information, I highly suggest you to watch that video from the Solange te parle channel. She is a native Québécoise, so you can trust what she says. Most videos made by French people who teach “how to speak Québécois” are mostly bad, even insulting sometimes. This one is very good though. *I am in a café right now, so I can’t record myself, but I’ll do it when I’ll get back home so you can understand better what I’m talking about. The pronunciation of D/T A Québécois will pronounce D and T as affricate consonants in front of the vowels U and I. It means a [s] or [z] sound is going to be added. dinosaure → dZinosaure durable → dZurable tulipe → tSulipe tisane → tSisane This is something other Francophones don’t do and it’s actually very hard for a Québécois not to do it. When I try, I feel ridiculous. No, wait, I actually feel posh haha (which makes me feel ridiculous). Vocaroo | Voice message I did the Québécois pronunciation twice for each word, then the “French” pronunciation once. I put “French” between quotation marks because it really feels like I butchered these words haha! It’s horrible for me not to affricate the consonants. Four nasal vowels Québécois French has four nasal vowels, which is not the case from most varieties. [ɑ̃] → sans, vent, septembre [ɛ̃] → vin, timbre, main, daim, plein, lynx, thym, chien [ɔ̃] → son [œ̃] → brun, parfum You see the last one? It’s the one that doesn’t exist in all varieties. This means a French speaker from France is most likely going to pronounce “brin” and “brun” the same way, although any native French speaker from Québec is going to pronounce these words differently. Vocaroo | Voice message I pronounced “brun” and “brin” with my Québécois accent twice, then I pronounced these two words like a lot of French speakers would (as you may hear, it’s twice the same pronunciation). Distinction between “j’aimerai” and “j’aimerais” Not all French varieties from France differenciate the verb endings “ais” and “ai”, which means the futur simple and conditionnel présent often sound the same. You can hear it very well in the song “Belle”. One of the three singers is from France (Patrick Fiori) and at some point, the lyrics are: “Quel est l’homme qui détournerait son regard d’elle?”. Patrick Fiori doesn’t pronounce “détournerait” the same way a Québécois would. Vocaroo | Voice message I pronounced “j’aimerais\j’aimerai” and “je serais\je serai” (twice each) as Québécois pronounce it. Diphtong vowels Québécois often don’t pronounce È and Ê the same way. That statement is true for A and Â too. A Québécois will pronounce Ê and Â with a diphtong in it. It means “tâche/tache” and “faites/fête” are not pronounced the same way in Québec, but it usually is in most varieties. Ê → [ɛː] (aè) Â → [ɑ] I already wrote an answer about that, you can read it here and hear the pronunciation: Mylène Truchon's answer to In a French context, how is “è” pronounced differently from “ê”? Speakers from Montréal usually create very strong diphtongs. A lot of French people actually only visit Montréal and takes from granted this is “Québécois French”, but it’s actually more “Montréal French” (or “South-West of Québec French”). You can hear what this sounds like by listening to Émile Bilodeau’s songs. He has a very thick accent. Even I am shocked by his accent! :P If you speak French, you can also read more about it here: Cartographier la rivalité linguistique entre Québec et Montréal. As you can see on the following maps, the very strong diphtong (purple on the map) is much more common in the West-South of Québec. The pronunciation of the final T This is not common everywhere, but some French speakers from France pronounce the final T in a lot of words, like “août”, which they pronounce [ut] (“oute”). A Québécois pronounces [u] (“ou”). Vocaroo | Voice message I pronounced “le mois d’août” twice with my normal accent, then twice with the French accent.

I don’t think I would be able to guess a student nationality by reading his/her text, but as I said, there are definitely some types of mistakes directly linked with some nationalities/native languages.

Question: What are some examples of propaganda in literature?
Answer: The socialist realism in Soviet Union The socialist realism genre is an example of literature used for propaganda. As it states in the Wikipedia article: Socialist realism is a style of idealized realistic art that was developed in the Soviet Union and was imposed as the official style in that country between 1932 and 1988 […]. Socialist realism is characterized by the glorified depiction of communist values, such as the emancipation of the proletariat, by means of realistic imagery. Staline (and Nicolae Ceausescu, in Romania) wanted to create what was called “The New Man”. The main ways to reeducate were the work and the collectivity (by and for the collectivity). To set examples, authors were ordered to write a certain type of literature. The story was almost always the same. It could be about a rebel who became a national hero after getting new social values. Or a martyr suffering for the community. The important thing is, in the end, it has to show that sacrifice is great. The roman du terroir in Québec The expression roman du terroir is used in Québec to talk about a type of literature that used to be very present in Québec before 1945: It had as its goal the celebration of rural life during a period of rapid industrialization. The clergy and the state encouraged this type of literature […] The Québécois establishment were hoping that support for this type of novel would strengthen Québécois morality, and perhaps halt an exodus of French Québécois from rural farming areas to Montreal and the textile factories of New England. The main values of romans du terroir were set out by people like Henri-Raymond Casgrain and Lionel Groulx, men of faith, and were: It says it lasted until 1945, but you should know that at some point, a lot of “anti-terroir” books were written. These books actually showed that life in rurality wasn’t as good as the other books pretended. Of famous example is La Scouine by Albert Laberge. Another funny thing: the most well-known roman du terroir is probably Maria Chapdelaine, written by Louis Hémon, who visited from France. He wrote that book as a caricature of romans du terroir, but it became the most famous one.

Question: What are some interesting psychological experiments?
Answer: One of my favourite experiments ever is the one made for the documentary Le jeu de la mort. You can find the whole documentary on Youtube, but it’s in French. The Milgram experiment It’s a copycat of the Milgram experiment. If you don’t know what it is, look at the picture below and read the text (from Wikipedia): The experimenter (E) orders the teacher (T), the subject of the experiment, to give what the latter believes are painful electric shocks to a learner (L), who is actually an actor and confederate. The subject is led to believe that for each wrong answer, the learner was receiving actual electric shocks, though in reality there were no such punishments. Being separated from the subject, the confederate set up a tape recorder integrated with the electro-shock generator, which played pre-recorded sounds for each shock level. The experiment was truly about testing obedience. The intensity of the fake electric shocks actually increased and they would have killed the learner had they been real. The experiment was in reaction of the German Nazi criminals. Today, we look at nazi and can’t believe about how evil they were, but would you have done differently had you been a German soldier? What Le jeu de la mort did differently In the Milgram experiment, the authority is a scientist. In Le jeu de la mort, the authority is television, and more precisely a female French TV host named Tania Young. The process was the same as the Milgram experiment (there was a teacher and a learner, and the learner was an actor), but this time, it was a fake TV show named La Zone Xtrême (The Extreme Zone). They actually got “better” results than the Milgram experiment. 81% of the participants completed the task, therefore killing Jean-Paul, the learner (the result was 62% in the Milgram experiment). It’s very interesting because we can see people feeling uncomfortable. Most of them know they’re doing something bad. They say it out loud. They say they want to stop, especially when Jean-Paul’s reactions become worrying, but yet, they continue and finish the task. They show common ways people react because they’re stressed. A lot of them laugh, because laughing is a good way to deal with stress. They also try to give the right answer to Jean-Paul in not so subtle ways (by saying the right example louder or slower, as examples). Some people, at the end, said: “I finished because I know it was not real, TV can’t kill people!”. How can they know? That’s a lot of trust they put in other people. What I learned from it I often talk about that documentary to my students. Some of them react by saying they would have walked out the experiment. They know as a fact they would have been a part of the 19% who were strong and courageous enough to stop the game. To be honest, they worry me the most. I think being that confident means you’re not worried, so you’re not careful. They also stop thinking about it: “Oh yeah I would have stopped”, and they don’t introspect. I personally don’t know if I would have been able to stop. I can’t pretend that I’m that good. I have been in situation in which I know I should have acted differently, like when I witnessed bullying. I now try to learn from my mistakes and I try to speak out loud when I get in these situations, but I will never pretend I’m above all that.

Question: In a French context, how is “è” pronounced differently from “ê”?
Answer: The “ê” is sometimes pronounced with a diphthong by some French speakers. The circumflex accent was originally there to show the letter must be pronounced differently and as much as that difference disappeared for a lot of words, it still exists for others, at least in Québec. It also shows there used to be a “s” in the word (“être” → “estre”, “île” → “isle”). A diphthong is when you pronounce two vowels, and in that situation, the “ê” is sometimes pronounced “aè”. edit: Or you can just pronounce it a little bit longer, but that is not exactly right. The best examples would probably be “fête” and “tête” because we can compare them with “faites” and “tète”. In the sentences: “Vous faites une fête.” and “Tu tètes la tête.” (this makes no sense, I know), the words are pronounced differently. I recorded myself so you can hear it: Vocaroo | Voice message In Québec, the “â” is also pronounced differently than the “a” in many words. In the sentence: “Regarde les pattes et les pâtes”, the words “pattes” and “pâtes” aren’t pronounced the same way: Vocaroo | Voice message However, if you come in Québec and pronounce “faites” and “fête” the same way, people won’t mind it, as much as I was never ridiculized for pronouncing them differently by French speakers who aren’t Québécois.

Question: Do you think it makes a difference learning French from a native French speaker from France compared to a French teacher from Quebec?
Answer: The French that is taught is from the “standard” register, which isn’t similar everywhere, but almost is. When I go to France, that is the register I use and people understand me very well. They hear my accent from Québec, but they can understand me nonetheless. My student also told me it was very easy to understand me when I speak to them. The pronunciation For the pronunciation, there are some differences, and you’ll learn some of them: These differences are usually not a problem when it’s time to understand French speakers from other regions, or when it’s time to be understood. There are also other differences, but teachers won’t teach them, like the pronunciation of the letters “t/d” in front of the vowels “u/i” (in Québec, we add a “s/z” sound, but it’s very subtle: tu vois le le dinosaure → tSu vois le dZinosaure). There are pronunciations “typically from Québec”, but as a French teacher, I don’t teach an accent, I teach the pronunciation, so if it is from the casual language, I won’t teach it. When I do, it’s because I want my students to understand these pronunciations, not to use them. I teach them to understand “chu content” (I am happy), but not to use it. I teach them to say “je suis” (I am) instead. The vocabulary This is the biggest difference between the French from France and Québec (and anywhere else by the way): the vocabulary. There are some words not used in France I definitely teach anyway. I don’t teach “faire les courses”, I teach “faire l’épicerie” (buy groceries). I don’t teach “faire du shopping”, I teach “magasiner” (to shop). And I don’t teach “petit-déjeuner/déjeuner/dîner”, I teach “déjeuner/dîner/souper” (names of the meals). However, most of the vocabulary you would learn in my class can be used in France, Belgium, Swiss, etc. But you should know there is no way a teacher can teach vocabulary that would be 100% universal, no matter what is the language, so what I just said about the vocabulary is true for every teacher from any country. For the words that are from the “slang” or are more casual, I teach the most popular ones, but I explain that they’re used in spoken French, not written French, like “être tanné” (to be sick of something), “fait que” (so), etc. Yet again, I mostly want my students to understand these words, not to use them (althoug they can use them when they talk if they want, I actually like it when they do). The final answer I read answers written here and they say: “French from Québec is different, so yes.” Lol what do you guys think I teach my students!? You think I teach them: “Toé pis moé on va-tu se frencher dans l’char?” Get a grip, guys. We teach standard French. As someone who learn French as a second language, you’ll never speak like a native, unless you get very good. Then you’ll be close to at best (if you move to Québec or a francophone country for many years, as an example). So the regional accent, the regional vocabulary and all that… you’ll likely actually never get it. What you’ll get is a French that is quite “standard” and can be spoken anywhere, so you shouldn’t care about “not being understood in France or Belgium because you learned French in Québec”. You should actually worry much more about the accent you get from you native language. I personally think that learning French in Québec instead of France is actually great because you’ll be familiar with more than one version of French because people from Québec are much more familiar with different versions of French than people from France are. As a teacher, I use material produced in Québec, in France, in Belgium, etc. I also am much more aware about the differences between the different versions of French, so are my students at the end of my class. And here is the thing: that idea you have about the French from France is very likely to be fake. There are a lot of accents and dialects in France. In Belgium, the accent is also different. In every country, there are a lot of accents and vocabulary and pronunciations that are different. And it’s true for other languages too by the way (English, Spanish, etc.). So, does it makes no difference to learn French from a Québécois? For you, as you are not a native speaker, not really. The differences will be small.

Question: Is the dictionary definition of feminism an accurate one? If not, why is it so broadly cited?
Answer: Language is not always an objective science and therefore, people often disagree on the meaning of words. The more abstract the concept, the more abstract the definition. Considering “feminism” is a theory, therefore is 100% abstract, the risks of disagreeing about its definition are very high. Feminists themselves don’t agree on most matters (and it’s normal). A lot of people then look in the dictionary, thinking they’ll find the truth there because they think dictionaries are objective. It’s not true at all, they are usually full of cultural conventions. As an example, a dictionary from Québec and a dictionary from France will probably have some differences since they study different cultural backgrounds. The era in which it was written will also have an influence. A dictionary must also give very concise definitions, and therefore some of them aren’t precise at all. The world is full of nuances and the dictionary can’t talk about these nuances. So is the definition of feminism an accurate one? Let’s say it is as accurate as a very short definition of a very complex topic can be.

The reason being I knew what was a mistake and what wasn’t, but I didn’t know why. So I had to learn more about the language system: the grammatical categories, the grammatical functions, the syntax rules, etc. Most of these were pretty basic though as most of the rules were innately known as I was a native speaker. In university, I started to get linguistic classes: grammar, syntax, history of the language, etc. I was then ready to teach. I started as a private tutor. French as a second language I would describe my first experience as a French as a foreign language teacher with this metaphor: it was like running straight into a wall. I had to learn EVERYTHING. I was already pretty good at understanding the French language as a native language, but I pretty much had to learn it as a second language. These all are thing I didn’t know about. They were innate to me, and to any native French speaker, but these people weren’t native speakers. So of course, I learned them. I found an amazing book, Grammaire française by Jacqueline Ollivier. And now, I learn a foreign language (German) so I can understand the struggle of my students. This way, I feel I can be a better teacher because I have to find solutions for myself, therefore I can give them these solutions to help them. The biggest misconception about language teaching is that native speakers are the best teachers. It is not true, unless that person studied her/his language as a second language. I think I am now a competent teacher, but at first, I was VERY bad. Knowing your language as a native or as a foreign language are two totally different things. And teaching language is a very complex processus too. There are a lot of competences to think about: listening/speaking/reading, syntax/grammar/vocabulary/pronunciation, etc. I have mostly taught to intermediate students. Question: Were Quentin Tarantino's films feminist?
Answer: Koyel Bandyopadhyay's answer is very interesting and my answer is going to echo hers. I was reading what she wrote and it made me think a lot about something I once talked about in a seminar. Her answer is very interesting and I don’t disagree with it, but I wanted to show the other side of the medal. My original analysis was about The Walking Dead comic book, so I am going to compare Tarantino’s and Kirkman’s works. This will not be a very analytic answer, as I mostly want to give analysis tracks. Active VS passive characters Claude Bremond wrote that we are usually able to find a few categories in which it’s possible to classify characters, the main one being: active VS passive. Women are often in the second category: they can’t or they don’t want to act. My master degree was about The Walking Dead and I showed how most women from the 18 first volumes of the comic book are in the second category. As much as a passive female character does not automatically equals sexism, it’s alarming how much, in action movies and books, women are often unable to do anything compare to their male counterparts. So the fact Quentin Tarantino shows highly active female characters is a proof that his scenarios may be less sexist than a majority of Hollywood movies. Women with weapons Sarah Burke wrote: Well, to put it simply and without diving into a whole lot of critical theory (see Freud and Butler for that), in our male dominated society, men are usually the sole owners and wielders of weapons. Thus, when we see women owning and using these weapons it can read as a transgressive act. (Burke, 2013) In Quentin Tarantino’s movies, women are very often seen using weapons, and that’s not it. They are often very good and deadly when in possession in these weapons. In The Walking Dead, most women who try to use weapons are unable to, even when they are taught to use those weapons. In her book Les femmes d’action au cinéma, Raphaëlle Moine said: En se jetant physiquement dans l’action, les femmes empruntent aux hommes les armes, les machines et les techniques de mort qu’ils ont inventées et dont ils sont les utilisateurs traditionnels. La violence des femmes d’action s’écarte ainsi de la forme conventionnelle et misogyne de l’hystérie féminine. (Moine, 2010: 106) By physically throwing themselves in the action, women take the men’s weapons, the machines and the deadly techniques they invented and which they usually are the sole users. The violence of these action women is then different to the conventional and misogynistic feminine hysteria. The rape and revenge scenario Koyel talked about this one. In movies and books, women are often victims of the male violence. When this happens, we can observe two different types of scenarios: Kill Bill is one of the best examples. Many feminists dislike these types of scenario, and I don’t think they are wrong. Melissa Hugel’s The trouble with rape revenge movies is a proof. Howerer, I do like Virginie Despentes’ from King Kong Théorie explanation: Quand des hommes mettent en scène des personnages de femmes, c’est rarement dans le but d’essayer de comprendre ce qu’elles vivent et ressentent en tant que femmes. C’est plutôt une façon de mettre en scène leur sensibilité d’hommes, dans un corps de femme. [...] Le message qu’ils nous font passer est clair: comment ça se fait que vous ne vous défendez pas plus brutalement? Ce qui est étonnant, effectivement, c’est qu’on ne réagisse pas comme ça. Une entreprise politique ancestrale, implacable, apprend aux femmes à ne pas se défendre. (Despentes, 2006: 45-46) When men create female characters, it’s rarely because they want to understand what goes through their head or what their feelings are about. It is instead to show their male’s point of view, but in a woman’s body. […] The message they want to tell us is clear: why don’t you defend yourself more violently? It is indeed weird that we don’t react this way. It is because a relentless ancestral policy teaches women not to defend themselves. The body of action movie female characters In her book Les femmes d’action, Raphaëlle Moine talks about the physical attributes of action women. She says we can see two types of women: the tough women, with athletical and fit bodies, and the babes in arms, who are glamors and hyperfeminine. They think the last ones are actually a representation of a male fantasy, but the first ones are actually “real” fighters, shaped by “hard work”. Honestly, about that one, I don’t think Quentin Tarantino gets a high feminist score, but I haven’t seen all of his movies and it has been a while for a few of them.

In the 19th century, the Anglo-Canadians dominated the most important sectors (politic, economy, etc.), therefore it was said by the Church that a higher birth rate in Quebec would be a way to fight the British discrimination and immigration, since Québécois (who speak French) would now be in such a high number. Families were pressured to get more children. Since the “Révolution tranquille” (Quiet Revolution), the era Québec became much more progressist, the birth rate is now much more lower. Question: Why is French spelling so irrational and unsystematic? Why don't they change it?
Answer: The French spelling is indeed irrational and unsystematic quite often. However, some spellings may seem irrational, but actually aren’t. Some examples of rational, but seemingly irrational spellings So many things, in the French language, can be explained by studying the history of it. You can also look at the “etymology”, which is the origin of the word. In French, a lot of words come from the latin, so some spellings are also explained by that. The final silent consonant are usually there for that reason. Some examples of irrational spellings Some spellings are however very artificial. One example of that would be “poids/pois/poix”. These words are spelled differently so we can make the difference between them. Another example would be the addition of “etymologic letters” so some words would appear more latin. At some point, many people wanted to protect latin, so they tried to make French appear more latin by adding some letters. I sadly don’t have any example coming at the top of my head. Why don’t we do anything about it? People are very conservative. In 1990, a reform was made in the French language. Some spellings were changed. The most famous word is “oignon”, that would now be written “ognon”, or “nénuphar”, that would now be written “nénufar”. Most people complained. The first reason, I believe, is that people learned some things and they didn’t want to unlearn them. The second reason is that many people think these modifications were the proof that we are getting dumber (“Kids can’t even learn French properly, we have to make it easier for them! Pfff!”). Another reason I heard, but quite rarely, was that many spellings, like I showed sooner, are explained by history and that by changing these spellings, we erase history. Strangely though, I often hear people saying: “French is so illogical!”, but then they also complain about the reform from 1990. Some have fair criticisms and I don’t pretend the reform is 100% good, but many complain about it without even knowing what it is. I know because I used to be one of these people, when I was much younger. ;) You have to know that French people are also usually very conservative. Recently, the idea of making French more “gender neutral” was discussed. In France, some people talked about having feminine forms for the words describing jobs. Many French people didn’t want to, they talked against it and really didn’t want an “avocat” (a lawyer) to be an “avocate” (a female lawyer) when the person is female, but in Québec, we have been doing that for years! In France, though, they don’t do that yet. You should also know that changing a language is very long. You can’t just learn something to people, then someday tell them: “Yo, we changed everything, so learn these new things now.” People definitely won’t.

Question: Should I learn French with an African? How different is it apart the standard French?
Answer: Short answer: yes, you should. Long answer: French can be spoken with different “registers”. Some people say these registers tells the quality of the spoken French. There are three registers: Most people think the consultative register is a universal language spoken in every French speaking countries and that if you learn it, you will be able to be understood anywhere and you’ll never have any problem. It is not true. It is ALMOST true. Because here is the important thing to understand: there is not ONE French language, there are MANY French languages. Before you panic, understand this: the same thing can be told about English, Spanish, etc. If you go to the UK, Canada, the USA and Australia, do you think they’ll all speak exactly the same English? No. Will they understand each others if they try? Yes. Will they sometimes get mixed up anyway? Yes, because it’s impossible for them to speak EXACTLY the same language. As an example, what is a “jumper”? An American is likely to tell you it is a dress you wear on top of a blouse. A British will tell you it is a sweater. And “jumper” is not a word you find in the casual register. It is from the consultative register. So, how is this possible? Every form of the French, English, Spanish (etc.) languages have what is usually recognize as its standard register. These registers are usually pretty close to each others, but they aren’t 100% similar. So there is not ONE standard French language, there are many standard French language. So should you learn French from an African? Yes. Should you learn French from a French? Yes. Should you learn French from a Quebecer? Yes. Should you learn French from a Belgian? Yes. Should you learn French from a Swiss? Yes. Not one of them is going to teach you French better than the other. They will all teach you their version of standard French, and that version, although it won’t be similar to the others, will be close enough for you to understand most of the things the other speakers will tell you. There is not one version that is the “pure” version. An example of that is that a French teacher will tell you that the meals we eat are: “petit-déjeuner”, “déjeuner” and “dîner”. A teacher from Belgium, Swiss, Congo, Rwanda, Burundi, Quebec (etc.) will teach you the meals are called: “déjeuner”, “dîner” and “souper”. The dictionary tells you the latter form is the “regional” or “ancient” version, therefore that the French version is the good one, but the truth is the French seem to be the ones who are different (in some French regions, they also use the latter). So although the dictionary does judge these forms are “incorrect”, it is not a realistic judgement. So do not think French teachers are the ones who are always right and that they have the universal version of French.

Question: What is the difference between "bien" and "bon" in French?
Answer: “bon/mauvais” are adjectives: they add information about nouns → “un bon ami”, “une mauvaise voiture”… We also use them to talk about a talent, or the lack of a talent: “Je suis bon à la flûte.”, “Je suis mauvaise au piano.”… We also use them to talk about the taste or something you can smell: “La tarte est bonne.”, “Ce parfum a une mauvaise odeur.”… → In that situation, they can be adverbs (so they are invariable) if we use them to change the verbs “goûter” (to taste) and “sentir” (to smell): “Elle goûte bon.” or “Ils sentent mauvais.” With the verb “être” (to be), we use them to say that we like something quite a lot: “Ce film est bon.”, “Cette chanson est mauvaise.”… “bien/mal” are adverbs: they add information about verbs → “Ils chantent mal.”, “Tu parles bien.”… We also use them to talk about the morality or the “legal state” of something: “Voler est mal.”, “Aider les personnes âgées est bien.”… With the verb “être” (to be), we use “bien” (but not “mal”) to say we kind of like something, that is was only okay: “Ce film est bien.”, “Cette chanson est bien.”… “bien” is also an adverb that means “a lot” → “Il mange bien trop.”, “Tu es bien content!”…

However, for speakers who are not native, it is very different. Native speakers know that the feminine/masculine system is very hard for people who don’t have French as a first langage, so most of them don’t mind at all if mistakes are made. They might correct you, but not because you insult them. They simply want to help you so you won’t make that mistake again.

Question: What does informal Québécois look like in contrast to informal French from France?

We then conjugate it as a French verb: je me parke, tu te parkes, il se parke, etc. This is not something French people do, I believe. Another thing we do is that we translate English expression. In Québec, people say: “ça fait du sens”. It is the translation of “it makes sense”, because the French expression is actually “ça a du sens” (it has sense). Question: What method of learning finally enabled you to pronounce the French R?
Answer: The difference between the English and the French pronunciation of the R letter is mainly the position of the tongue. When pronouncing the French R, the tongue doesn’t touch the palate. Look at the picture on the left. The tip of the tongue is at the bottom of the mouth. When pronouncing the English R, the tongue touches the palate, or almost touches it, and the tip is at the top of the mouth. When teaching the pronunciation of the letter R to English speakers, I tell them to keep their tongue completely at the bottom of their mouth and I ask them to pronounce words with the sound of the R: reçu, rire, etc. They must absolutely keep the tongue at the bottom of the mouth, even if it is not comfortable. Some people can’t do that, so I tell them to hold a pencil inside their mouth. This way, their tongue is blocked. They practice this way with many words and for a while. Some of them then get it and it becomes more natural for them.

Question: Why do we say “Où est ma fenetre” but “Où est mon horloge” when both “fenetre” and “horloge” are feminine in French?
Answer: “mon” is used in front of a masculine noun, or in front of a feminine word starting with a vowel or a mute “h”. It's because there are rarely two vowel sounds back to back in French. There are indeed two types of “h” in French: the mute “h” and the aspirated “h”. The pronunciation is the same tough, it's the origin of the word that is different. The words with the aspirated “h” have Germanic origins. There are only a few word with that “h”, like “hache” (axe). So… ma copine mon amie mon horloge ma hache (all feminine words)

You can even kill characters and the story continues anyway, so the story depends on your performance. The lenght is also an important factor although TV shows are now a good solution to that problem. So the answer is mainly because in a video game, a huge part of the fun is the player being directly involved in the story instead of just being passive and looking at it. Just take a look at games made by TellTale studio. The player actually have little control on the story and there aren’t that much gameplay, so when they fail to present amazing scenarios, the games get bad reviews. You want to sell a cheap scenario? Question: What is horror? And how does it work?
Answer: Horror is a feeling It is a extreme form of fear, like terror. Since English isn’t my first language, I’ll quote my friend, Ms. Wikipedia, who is way better than me in English: Terror is usually described as the feeling of dread and anticipation that [may precede an] horrifying experience. By contrast, horror is the feeling of revulsion that usually occurs after something frightening is seen, heard, or otherwise experienced. It is the feeling one gets after coming to an awful realization or experiencing a deeply unpleasant occurrence. In other words, horror is more related to being shocked or scared (being horrified), while terror is more related to being anxious or fearful. Horror is also a fictional genre People don’t agree on what would be the exact definition of it, but generally it relies on horrifying situations to frighten the audience. To achieve that goal, there are many path that can be taken. Here are some. H.P. Lovecraft, one of the most famous horror theorists, said: “The oldest and strongest emotion of mankind is fear, and the oldest and strongest kind of fear is fear of the unknown” In French, we call it inquiétante étrangeté (worrying strangeness). In German (the concept was coined by Freud), it is call das Unheimliche (the strangeness). It’s showing objects in unfamiliar situations. A trope is a commonly recurring motif in a creative work. Many of our fears come from the society and the era we’re from. Therefore, we share many fears we others. As an example, in many societies, there are a lot of people scared of ghosts. Are many people scared of… pencils? Not really. Therefore, it would be more efficient to write a book about ghosts than about pencils. When a tropes is used in many horror stories, there are chances the audience will recognizes it and becomes worried. It’s important not to use too many tropes though. The story would then be cliché. Fear isn’t a comfortable feeling. When we’re scared, we don’t feel safe anymore. When someone doesn’t feel safe, he becomes paranoiac, which is good for a horror story. Movies and books can achieve that, but I believe that creepypastas are the best medium for that. You’ll read a book, but you’ll know it’s a book. It won’t hurt you. Same thing with movies. But when you read creepypastas on your computer, there might be some realistic thoughts that come to your mind: someone (or something) could control your computer. It could use it to communicate with you. It could use the camera to look at you. So you feel less safe. Once, I was reading a creepypasta called How to play alone. It was about things to do to “play” with a surnatural entity. In the comments, there were people explaining that they tried some of the things and shat their pants when they realised it worked. So the story felt more real. Found footage movies are also made to appear more real. This is supposedly real pictures, not a reconstitution. Finally, here is a quote by Stephen King. The 3 types of terror The Gross-out: the sight of a severed head tumbling down a flight of stairs, it's when the lights go out and something green and slimy splatters against your arm. The Horror: the unnatural, spiders the size of bears, the dead waking up and walking around, it's when the lights go out and something with claws grabs you by the arm. And the last and worse one: Terror, when you come home and notice everything you own had been taken away and replaced by an exact substitute. It's when the lights go out and you feel something behind you, you hear it, you feel its breath against your ear, but when you turn around, there's nothing there...

Question: When did the French start to talk in French?
Answer: A quick history of the French language I already wrote on Quora. France used to be named “Gaul”. People living there were “Gallics” until they got invaded by Romans. Gallics were forced to speak Latin (vulgar Latin), but the truth is Gallics didn’t totally abandon their language, thus it kind of got mixed with the vulgar Latin. The Germans then invaded the Gaul (that was now in the Roman empire), but they couldn’t really get people to speak their germanic language for a couple reasons: the Latin was seen as more noble and many Germans, due to the fact there weren’t that many of them, married Gallo-Romans and it was easier for their children to learn the native language of Gaul. The Oaths of Strasbourg (Les Serments de Strasbourg), an alliance between three kings who signed it in 842, is considered as the earliest official texts in which the “French” language appears (most precisely, Gallo-Romance, which is “old French”). In 1539, Ordinance of Villers-Cotterêts (Ordonnance de Villers-Cotterêts) was signed by Francis I of France. It is the oldest French legislation and it stated that French would now be the official language in many government, judicial and ecclesiastical matters.

Question: Why do mostly girls become ghosts in horror movies?

Have you ever heard of das Unheimliche, a German word? It was coined by Freud. In English, the word is “uncanny”. This is when an object is used in an unsettling context, which provokes discomfort. So… Ghosts are seen as a threat. Women and children are seen as vulnerable. Therefore, to see a woman or a child as a threat is uncanny. It provokes discomfort. That is probably why so many ghost figures are women or children. It also became a cliché, a trope. It is effective since horror also relies on a system of commonly used representations. An example of a trope vastly used in horror movies is scenes in which the character looks at himself/herself in a mirror and something appears behind him. This is actually so common that, I don’t know for you, but I get scared automatically when someone, in a horror movie, looks at itself in a mirror. For a writer, it makes the job much easier to use a few tropes (but it becomes comical or predictable when there are too many). Also, host movies are often about revenge. Well, scenarios showing women who seek for revenge are very common. There is actually a genre named “rape and revenge”. A woman get raped and… seeks for revenge. So this is another cliché that the viewer understand very quickly: a woman seeking for revenge. That is also another reason why so many ghosts are female. Violence against children and women is also generally seen as VERY unacceptable. It is judged more severely than violence against men. So when a child or a woman seeks for revenge, we think that what happens against them is so unethical that it makes sense that the revenge is so extreme.

Question: What is the French public's opinion of the Académie Française?
Answer: I am not from France, but when I studied linguistic and literature, the common opinion was that the Adadémie française was quite puristic and attached to the tradition, which wasn’t seen as a good thing. It’s normal for a language to change, but for some, it is seen as a disaster. Recently, I discovered why we conjugate the past participle used with the “to have” auxiliary the way we do in French. Basically, Clément Marot, a poet from Renaissance, liked Italy and therefore decided that the rule should be the same as in Italian (the king François Ier asked him to chose what would be the rule). Funny thing is he misunderstood that rule. So basically, we’re stuck with that rule that doesn’t make much sense because of him. However, Georges Leygues, in the 1900’s, tried to change it, but the Académie said NO. It wasn’t surprising because that is what they do best: saying NO. Gérard Briais’ comparison is very good: they’re the language Catholic Church. In Québec, we have OQLF which, I believe, despite not being perfect and making their own mistakes, is much more modern.

Question: What is the difference between a traveller and a tourist?
Answer: These questions and the answers always make me raise a brow, especially since there are generally a judgement that is made upon each of these categories: “tourist” is so bad, but “traveller” is great! I read a few definitions both given here or elsewhere and they always talk about how a traveller is free, learn the language, learn the customs, is such an adventurer, etc. Tourists, on the other hand, crawl from a touristic site to another one, expect everyone to speak their language, sleep in a comfortable bed (how dare they!), etc. Here is a thing: looking at these definitions, I’m always BOTH. And I’m sure everyone is. I’m in a new country for goat sakes. I always end up with my huge map in my hand (I still use printed maps), trying to find the way and asking people what is the way. I don’t care if I don’t look like a local: I AM NOT ONE. Also, let’s take an example. I spent three days in Bruges (Belgium). The language spoken there is mainly Flemish. So I learned: I also learned “sorry” and “I don’t speak Flemish” (but I’ve forgotten how to say it now). That’s pretty cute, but the truth is I ended up speaking English or French all the time because 4 words-ish isn’t enough to speak a language. I mean… no offense, but I won’t learn Flemish because I was there for 3 days. Also, of course I’ll visit the main touristic attractions. The Eiffel tower? Check. The Manneken-Pis? Check. I have a friend who didn’t want to visit these places when she travelled because they were “so touristic”. Too bad for you, they’re usually popular for a reason. Most of them were great (okay, the Manneken-Pis wasn’t haha). Plus, they are symbols. They’re kind of a reality check: “Yep, you’re truly in Paris, look, here is the Eiffel tower!” “Guided tours are so touristic!” Well, I love them (not too many though), especially the ones in which you get to walk around for a couple hours and use the public transportations. They lead me to places I would have looked at and not really cared about. Now, I have a guide to explain to me why that place is interesting and its history! Plus they usually have good adresses for restaurants and bars (never been disappointed listening to their advices). I also read about how going to Mc Donald’s is touristic. But… I like going to Mc Donald’s to see the differences in the menu since Mc Donald’s adapts it to the cultures. To me, it is a cultural experience actually. ;) I do all these things, but I always end up trying the local cuisine too, speaking with locals, going to shows, sport events, theater, etc. So my travels weren’t less interesting nonetheless. I still lived an adventure, I still got in touch with the locals, I still got lost, I still admired the beauty… even though I took selfies! So what is the difference between a tourist and a traveller? To me, there are none. Each one get to experiment his/her trip the way he/she wants and is pleased and no judgement should be made (except if that person is an arsehole, of course). It doesn’t mean the trip was less of an adventure. It doesn’t mean you don’t get to discover the culture. Question: What languages are the hardest to learn as a new language? Is English considered an easy language to learn?
Answer: There are many things we must think about before answering this question. What is the speaker’s mother tongue? My native language is French, therefore learning Spanish, Catalan, Romanian or Italian are going to be easier for me than for an English speaker, for example, since they share similar roots. Grammar, vocabulary and pronunciation German has a fairly difficult grammar, but the pronunciation is very regular thus easy to learn. On the other side, English has a fairly easy grammar, but the pronunciation is very irregular thus harder to learn. You want an example? Pronounce “ear”, “heard” and “bear”. The letters “ear” aren’t pronounced the same way in any of these three words. What is the speaker’s access to the culture? The best way to learn a language is to immerse yourself in that language. An English learner will find plenty of things to read, watch or listen to since English has a huge cultural background. It’s pretty mainstream. However, let’s imagine I want to speak German. I don’t say the German cultural production is small or uninteresting, but as a Canadian, I have a smaller access to it. I must dig deeper to find it. Of course, some language are “objectively” easier or harder to learn than some (as an example, Spanish is, for most people, easier to learn than French), but when you ask which languages are harder to learn, this ain’t a question that can totally be answered without knowing some things about you beforehand.

Question: Why does French from France or from Paris sound so much better than French made in Quebec?

But as much as I disagree with you, I can try to guide you a little bit. Also, there are more than one French accent in France, so I’ll answer talking about a “standard” Parisian French (the one you’ll hear watching the news). In France, people tend to pronounce more than in Québec. They pronounce every syllable, which isn’t true in Québec. “Il ne vient plus.” in France will sound “Y vient pu” in Québec. The mouth muscles are also more relaxed while speaking the French from Québec. It is especially true when we pronounce the letter “t” in front of the letter “i” and “u”, because the “t” is then pronounced “ts”. The mouth has less often a “O” shape. In short, the French enunciate more. But we have an expression here to talk about people who don’t enunciate enough: “That person talks as if she/he had a hot potato in her/his mouth.” And I want to finish by saying that I love the French spoken here, in Québec. <3

You have to be able to answer this question: “Why do I say it that way?” As an example, why do you say: “Qu’est-ce que tu aimes?”, but “Qu’est-ce qui te plaît?”. This one is a hard one, but here is the thing: make sure that you AT LEAST know what is a verb, a noun, an adjectif, a preposition, a conjunction, etc. Finally, here is a website that may help you: CCDMD. Question: As a beginner for learning French, how do I memorize words effectively and learn to actually use them in daily life?
Answer: Websites like Duolingo are quite good to help your learn vocabulary. I used it with German and it was quite effective. The only thing I didn’t like about it was that I couldn’t pick the words I would learn and I didn’t always agree with the choice that were made. I lost my mind when I saw the website tried to make me learn “käfer” (“beetle”). You can use little piece of cardboard and make a memory game out of it. A little advice, use different colours for the masculine and feminine words. Yes, it isn’t that bad if you mix the gender of the words, but this is an easy way to actually not mix it. If you’re not much into crafting, you can use Anki, but honestly, cardboard pieces are better. Write articles. Talk about your life, your job, your hobbies, etc. (things you’ll probably talk a lot about). Lang-8 is a cool website for that. French speakers may correct your mistakes. I personally use Quora to improve my English and it works greatly. Since I write mostly about my interests, I learn new vocabulary that is obviously very helpful for me. Give yourself an objective. Tell yourself: I will learn 20 new words a week, as an example. Then, at the end of the week, test yourself. And don’t forget: feedbacks are very important. Once you remember a word, don’t just put it aside and never think about it again. Here is a website I like using a lot as a teacher: point du FLE. I picked the “Jeux de vocabulaire” (vocabulary games) for you. Videogames can be great too. I heard about In.fluent, but I don’t know how good it is. You could buy games for kids and play it or even play The Sims in French! Many basic words are used in that game. I wish you the best of luck. :)
